tool.name: HTML
tool.tagline: The markup language that gives every web page its structure and meaning
tool.description: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes the content of a web page: headings, text, links, images, forms and the regions of a layout. Browsers parse it into the DOM that CSS styles and JavaScript scripts. Writing clean, semantic HTML is the foundation of accessible, fast and search-friendly websites.

glossary.def:
A marker in angle brackets that starts or ends an HTML element, such as

to start a paragraph and

to end it.
An HTML attribute that is switched on just by being present, like disabled in <input disabled>. Its value doesn't matter; remove it to switch it off.
An HTML attribute that works on every element, such as id, class, hidden, title and lang.
A code that stands for a character in HTML text, written with & in front and ; after, such as the codes for < and & themselves.
A mode browsers use for pages without <!DOCTYPE html>: they copy the layout mistakes of very old browsers. With the doctype, pages get standards mode.
Short for character set: the encoding a page's text is stored in, declared in HTML with <meta charset="utf-8">.

In HTML layout, a block element (such as

or

) starts on a new line and stretches across the full width, unlike an inline element that sits inside text.

In HTML, the <header> element holds the introduction at the top of a page or section; in a table, a header cell (<th>) labels a row or column; in web traffic, a labelled line of extra information sent with a request or page.
Software or devices that help disabled people use a computer, such as screen readers that read pages aloud, or switches and voice control instead of a mouse.
The name a screen reader announces for a button, link or field, taken from its text, its label, its alt text or an aria-label.
In an HTML form, the pattern attribute: a regular expression the field's whole value must match before the form can be sent.
In an HTML form, a rule a field's value must follow, such as required, a minimum length or a pattern; the browser checks it before sending the form.
The browser's built-in checking of form fields against their rules (required, pattern, min, max...), which JavaScript can also read and control.
A part of a page marked with aria-live or role="alert" whose new text screen readers announce automatically, without the user moving there.
The small icon a browser shows on a page's tab and in bookmarks.
An attribute on and listing several versions of an image, so the browser can download the one that suits the screen.
Showing a differently cropped or composed image on different screen sizes, such as a tall crop on phones, using <picture>.
A simple text file format for video captions and subtitles, loaded with the <track> element.
A special layer above everything else on a page, used by modal dialogs and popovers, so nothing can cover them.
Closing a popup by clicking anywhere outside it or pressing Escape, as auto popovers do.
A part of the browser that reads ahead in the HTML while the page is still being built, to start downloading images, scripts and styles early.
A file the browser must finish downloading (and, for scripts, running) before it can carry on building or drawing the page, like CSS in the head.
The steps a browser takes from receiving HTML to drawing the first pixels: read the HTML, load the CSS, run blocking scripts, work out the layout, paint.
A form attribute choosing how the browser packs the fields when sending them; file uploads need enctype="multipart/form-data".
The HTML parser's rule for content that isn't allowed inside a table: it moves that content to just before the table.
The HTML parser's current state, such as 'in head' or 'in table', which decides what each tag it reads means.
The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines: the international standard for making websites usable by disabled people, used in many laws.
How much lighter text is than its background, from 1:1 (none) to 21:1 (black on white); accessible body text needs at least 4.5:1.
A <meta> element in a page's head that gives information about the page, such as its encoding, description or how to scale on phones.
The visible outline a browser draws around the link, button or field that keyboard input will go to.
A link path starting with /, like /about, which starts from the top folder of the current website.
The clickable words of a link. They should say where the link goes, because screen-reader users often hear links out of context.
The browser event that fires when the whole HTML page has been read and its elements built, before images finish loading.
A control that shows or hides a section when clicked, such as a <details> element with its <summary>.
The CSS Object Model: the browser's internal model of all the page's CSS rules, built from its stylesheets, much like the DOM is built from HTML.
The order in which pressing the Tab key moves between the links, buttons and fields of a page; by default, the order they appear in the HTML.
A link at the very top of a page that jumps straight to the main content, so keyboard users don't have to tab through the menu every time.
A checking tool built into Chrome's developer tools that scores a page for speed, accessibility and search-friendliness and lists problems.
Starting a video or audio clip automatically when the page loads; browsers only allow it for muted media unless the user has interacted.
A script attribute: the browser downloads the script while it reads the page, and runs it only after the whole page has been read, in page order.
Any file a web page loads besides the HTML itself: stylesheets, scripts, images, fonts, videos.
The text alternative for an image, written in the img element's alt attribute: read aloud by screen readers and shown if the image can't load.
The programming language that runs inside web pages, used to make them react to clicks and typing and to change their content.

concepts.name: Elements and attributes
concepts.summary: HTML labels each piece of a page with tags; tags make elements that sit inside each other, and attributes add extra details.
concepts.why: Every other HTML lesson is just a new element or attribute used with these same rules.
concepts.body:
Every **web page** you visit starts as a plain text file. A **browser** — the app you use to visit websites, such as Chrome, Firefox or Safari — downloads that file and turns it into the page you see. The file is written in **HTML** (HyperText Markup Language). HTML isn't a **programming language** (a language for giving a computer step-by-step instructions): it doesn't calculate anything. It labels pieces of content: "this is a heading", "this is a paragraph", "this is a link". The labels are **tags**: words in angle brackets. `

` starts a paragraph and `

`, with a slash, ends it. A start tag, the content and the end tag together make an **HTML element**: `

Some text

`. Elements can sit inside other elements, like folders inside folders, and must close in reverse order: `

hi

` is right, `

hi

` is not. A few elements can't hold any content, so they have no end tag: `` (an image), `
` (a line break), `` (a text field). You may see `
`; the slash is optional. An **attribute** adds extra information to an element. It goes inside the start tag as `name="value"`: `` says where a link goes, `` says which picture to show. Put values in double quotation marks. A **boolean attribute** is switched on just by being there: `` is disabled — and so is `disabled="false"`. Some **global attributes** work on any element: - `id` — a unique name for one element on the page, which links and code can point to. - `class` — one or more group names separated by spaces. **CSS**, the language that sets colours, fonts and layout, uses them to style groups of elements. - `hidden` hides the element; `title` adds a tooltip; `lang` sets the language of the text. - `data-*` such as `data-user-id="42"` stores your own data for JavaScript, the programming language that runs inside pages. Tag and attribute names aren't **case-sensitive**, but everyone writes them in lowercase. Because `<` starts a tag, showing a `<` or `&` sign in text needs a code called a **character reference**: `lt` or `amp`, written with `&` in front and `;` after.

takeaways:
A start tag, content and an end tag make an element: `

Hi

`
Elements sit inside each other and close in reverse order
Attributes go in the start tag as `name="value"`; boolean ones are on whenever present
`id` is unique on the page; a `class` can be shared by many elements
pitfalls: Writing `disabled="false"` and expecting the button or field to work — remove the attribute instead.

quiz.q: What does <input disabled="false"> show?
options: Nothing; it is removed as invalid
quiz.explain: A boolean attribute is on whenever it is present, whatever its value; remove it to enable the input.

concepts.name: Document structure
concepts.summary: Every page starts from the same skeleton: a doctype, an html element with a language, a head for information about the page, and a body for content.
concepts.why: Getting the skeleton right makes browsers use modern rules and read your text correctly in any language.
concepts.body:
Every HTML page starts with the same few lines. Think of them as the cover and contents page of a book: the reader never studies them, but everything depends on them.

- `<!DOCTYPE html>` comes first. It isn't an element, just a switch: without it, browsers fall back to **quirks mode**, where they copy the layout mistakes of 1990s browsers so very old pages still look the same.
- `<html lang="en">` wraps the whole page. Its `lang` attribute tells screen readers — apps that read the page aloud for blind users — how to pronounce the text, and helps translation tools and search engines.
- `<head>` holds information *about* the page, called **metadata**: the page title, links to CSS files, and more.
- `<body>` holds everything the visitor actually sees.

Inside a computer, text is stored as numbers, and the rule for turning numbers back into letters is called an **encoding**. Put `<meta charset="utf-8">` first in the head: **charset** is short for character set, and **UTF-8** is the encoding that covers every language and emoji. The browser needs to know it before reading any text, or accented letters can come out garbled.

The `<title>` is required, and matters more than it looks: it's the text on the browser tab, the default bookmark name, and usually the headline in search results.

Spaces and line breaks between your tags don't change the layout. In text, HTML squeezes any run of spaces, tabs and new lines — all called **whitespace** — into a single space, so indent your code however you like.

Save the file as `index.html` and open it in a browser. Then right-click the page and choose Inspect: the browser's developer tools show the tree of elements it built from your file.
concepts.code:
Hello, web

This paragraph is the visible content.
takeaways: Start every page with `<!DOCTYPE html>` so browsers use modern rules
head = information about the page; body = what visitors see
Put `<meta charset="utf-8">` first and set `lang` on `<html>`
pitfalls: Leaving out the doctype and then chasing strange layout problems caused by quirks mode.

quiz.q: What happens if a page leaves out <!DOCTYPE html>?
options: The browser shows it in quirks mode
quiz.explain: Without the doctype, browsers use quirks mode, which copies old browsers' layout behaviour.

quiz.q: Where does the text in <title> appear?
options: On the browser tab and in search results
As the first heading on the page
Nowhere; it is only for checking tools
At the bottom of the page
quiz.explain: The title labels the tab and bookmarks and is usually the headline in search results.

concepts.name: Headings, paragraphs and lists
concepts.summary: Structure text with headings h1 to h6, paragraphs, lists, and small elements for emphasis and code.
concepts.why: Headings and lists are how both readers and the tools blind users rely on skim a page.
concepts.body:
Text needs structure, and HTML has a small set of elements for it. **Headings** `

` to `

` form an outline, like the chapter and section titles of a report. Use one `

` for the page's main title, `

` for its sections and `

` for subsections, without skipping levels. Many blind people use a **screen reader**, an app that reads the page aloud, and they jump from heading to heading to find their way. Software like this, which helps disabled people use a computer, is called **assistive technology**. So pick a heading level by its place in the outline, never by the size you want; size is CSS's job. **Paragraphs** are `

`. Don't use empty paragraphs or `

` to make space; spacing is also CSS's job. Use `
` only for line breaks that belong to the content, like the lines of an address or a poem. **Lists** come in three kinds: - `

    ` for items in no particular order (shown with bullets) and `
      ` for numbered steps; each item goes in an `
    1. `. - `
      ` for terms and their descriptions, with `
      ` for each term and `
      ` for its description. - Lists can sit inside lists: put the inner `
        ` inside an `
      • `. Small elements mark up words inside a sentence: - `` for importance and `` for spoken emphasis. - `` for code, `` for keys to press, and `` for highlights. - `` for abbreviations, with the full form in `title`. `` and `` are for bold or italic text with no extra importance, like a product name or a foreign word. For quotations there is `
        ` for a quoted passage and `` for a short quote inside a sentence. `
        ` keeps spaces and line breaks exactly as typed.

Pick heading levels by structure, never by size
ul for unordered items, ol for steps, dl for terms and descriptions

Using `

` or empty `

` elements for spacing instead of CSS.

quiz.q: You want a smaller-looking section title under an h2. What should you use?
options: An h3, then set its size with CSS
A div with a big font
quiz.explain: The heading level reflects the outline; how it looks belongs to CSS.

concepts.name: Links
concepts.summary: Make links with the a element: to other pages, to a spot on the same page, to email addresses and to downloads.
concepts.why: Links are what make the web a web; getting addresses and link text right affects usability, search results and security.

Link text should describe where the link goes
Use `<a>` to go somewhere and `<button>` to do something

quiz.q: A page at https://site.com/blog/post.html has <a href="../about">. Where does it go?

concepts.name: Images
concepts.summary: Show pictures with img, always describe them with alt text, and give width and height so the page doesn't jump.
concepts.why: Images are most of what a page downloads, and missing alt text is the most common accessibility failure on the web.
concepts.body: `` puts an image on the page. It has no end tag, and two of its attributes deserve real thought. **alt** holds the image's **alt text**, a text alternative: screen readers read it aloud, and the browser shows it if the image fails to load. Describe what the image *tells* the reader in this context: "Bar chart: sales doubled in 2025", not "chart.png". If an image is pure decoration, write an empty `alt=""` so screen readers skip it. Leaving `alt` out entirely is worse: screen readers may read out the file name. **width and height** give the image's size in pixels, the tiny dots a screen is made of (write plain numbers, no "px"). They let the browser save the right amount of space before the image arrives. Without them, text jumps down as images load, and Google's page-quality scores count that against you. CSS can still resize the image; the browser uses the two numbers for its shape. Pick a file format to suit the picture: - JPEG, WebP or AVIF for photos; - PNG or WebP for screenshots and images with see-through parts; - SVG for logos, icons and diagrams, since it stays sharp at any size. For a caption, wrap the image in `
takeaways: Every img needs alt: a description, or `alt=""` if it's decoration
Set width and height so the page doesn't jump while images load
Use figure and figcaption for captions
`loading="lazy"` only for images far down the page
pitfalls: Lazy-loading the big image at the top of the page, which makes the most important picture appear later.

quiz.q: An icon next to the word 'Settings' inside a button is purely visual. What alt should it have?
quiz.explain: The word next to it already labels the button, so the icon is decoration and gets an empty alt.

concepts.name: Block, inline and generic containers
concepts.summary: See why some elements start a new line and others sit inside text, and when the plain div and span elements are the right choice.
concepts.why: Knowing how elements are laid out by default explains most surprises before you write any CSS.
concepts.body:
Look at any page and you'll see two kinds of element. Some, like paragraphs, sit on their own lines. Others, like a bold word, sit inside a line of text. - **Block** elements such as `

`, `

`, `
    `, `
    ` and `
    ` start on a new line and stretch across the full width available. - Inline elements such as ``, ``, ``, ``, `` and `` sit inside a line of text and are only as wide as their content. Each element has one of these behaviours by default; CSS can change it later. HTML also has rules about what may go inside what. A `

    ` may only contain inline content. If you put a `

    ` or a `
      ` inside a paragraph, the browser's **parser** — the part that reads your HTML and builds the page from it — ends the paragraph early, and you get an extra empty `

      ` you never wrote. Similarly, a `

        ` may only contain `
      • ` items directly. When no element describes your content, use the two plain wrapper elements: `
        ` (block) and `` (inline). They mean nothing at all; they exist so CSS and JavaScript have something to grab. That's their strength and their danger. A page built only from `
        `s can look fine, but it tells browsers, search engines and screen readers nothing about its structure. So reach for a meaningful element first — a heading, a list, a link, a button, `
        ` for menus or `
        ` for a story — and use `
        ` and `` only for grouping that's purely about looks, such as a wrapper you need for a layout or a span to colour one word.

concepts.name: Forms, inputs and labels
concepts.summary: Collect what users type with form, input, label and button, and send it to a server as name/value pairs.
concepts.why: Forms are how people sign up, search, pay and talk to almost every web app.
concepts.body:
A sign-up page, a search box, a checkout: all are **HTML forms**. A `<form>` groups the fields and sends their values when the user submits it.

Where do the values go? To a **server**: a computer that receives messages from browsers, called **requests**, and answers them. The form's `action` attribute is the URL to send to, and `method` says how:

- `method="get"` adds the values to the end of the URL after a `?`, like `/search?q=shoes`. That part of a URL is the **query string**. Use it for searches and filters.
- `method="post"` sends the values separately, inside the request rather than the URL. Use it for anything that changes data, like signing up.

Each field needs a `name`: only named fields are sent, as `name=value` pairs. The common fields:

- `<input type="text">` and its many other types (email, password, number, checkbox, radio...),
- `<textarea>` for several lines of text,
- `<select>` with `<option>` elements for a drop-down list,
- `<button>` to send the form.

Every field needs a **label**: the visible text saying what to type. You can wrap the field in a `<label>`, or give the label a `for` attribute matching the field's `id`. Screen readers read the label aloud, and clicking it puts the cursor in the field (or ticks the checkbox), which makes small targets easier to hit. A `placeholder` — grey hint text inside the field — is not a label: it disappears as soon as the user types.

Radio buttons that share a `name` form one group where only one can be chosen. Group related fields in a `<fieldset>`, with a `<legend>` stating the question.

A `<button>` inside a form sends the form by default. For a button that should only run JavaScript, write `type="button"`. Pressing Enter in a text field also sends the form.
concepts.code:
<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>

  <label>
    Password <input name="password" type="password" minlength="8" required>
  </label>

  <fieldset>
    <legend>Plan</legend>
    <label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="free" checked> Free</label>
    <label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="pro"> Pro</label>
  </fieldset>

  <label><input type="checkbox" name="news" value="yes"> Send me news</label>

  <button>Create account</button>   <!-- sends the form by default -->
</form>
<!-- Sends: email=...&password=...&plan=free (&news=yes only if ticked) -->
takeaways: Only fields with a name are sent
Every field needs a label (wrapping it, or for + id)
`method="get"` for searches, `method="post"` for changes
A button in a form sends it unless it has `type="button"`
pitfalls: Using placeholder text instead of a label.
A plain `<button>` meant for JavaScript accidentally sending the form.

quiz.q: A form has <input id="q"> with no name attribute. What is sent for it?
options: An error is shown to the user
quiz.explain: Only fields with a name are included in what the form sends.

concepts.name: Semantic page layout
concepts.summary: Use header, nav, main, article, section, aside and footer to describe the regions of a page instead of anonymous divs.
concepts.why: Landmark elements give screen-reader users a map of the page and make your HTML explain itself.
concepts.body:
HTML has elements for the typical regions of a page. They look exactly like `<div>` until styled, but they carry meaning.

- `<header>`: introductory content, usually a logo, site title and navigation. Can also head an article.
- `<nav>`: a block of major navigation links. Not every group of links: the main menu, a table of contents, page-number links.
- `<main>`: the page's primary content. Exactly one visible `<main>` per page, not inside header, footer or article.
- `<article>`: a complete piece that would make sense on its own: a blog post, a comment, a product card.
- `<section>`: a thematic group of content, normally with its own heading. If you can't think of a heading, you probably want a `<div>`.
- `<aside>`: tangentially related content, like a sidebar or callout.
- `<footer>`: closing information, such as copyright, contact links or an article's author info.

Browsers report many of these to screen readers as **landmarks**: a screen-reader user can jump straight to `main` or to the navigation, skipping repetitive content. `header` and `footer` count as page landmarks only when they aren't nested inside an article or section.

Other useful semantic elements are `<time datetime="2026-10-17">` for dates that programs can read, `<address>` for contact info of the page or article author, and `<search>` for a search region. Semantics also feed reader modes, browser features and search engines, so they pay off in many places at once.

One main per page
article = stands alone; section = themed part with a heading

quiz.q: Which element fits a single user comment under a blog post best?
quiz.explain: A comment is a complete piece of content that makes sense on its own, which is what article means.

concepts.name: Tables
concepts.summary: Present data in rows and columns with table, caption, thead, tbody, th and td, and mark header cells so screen readers announce them correctly.
concepts.why: Tables are the right tool for data with rows and columns, and the wrong tool for layout.
concepts.body:
A table is a grid: **rows** go across and **columns** go down. Use a `<table>` when data really fits a grid: a price list, a schedule, a comparison. Never use tables for page layout; that's CSS's job (its grid and flexbox tools).

The structure:

- `<caption>` as the first child gives the table a title, announced by screen readers.
- `<thead>`, `<tbody>` and `<tfoot>` group header, body and summary rows.
- `<tr>` is a row; `<th>` is a header cell and `<td>` a data cell.

Mark header cells with `<th>` and add `scope="col"` (labels its column) or `scope="row"` (labels its row), so assistive technology knows which data cells each header describes. When a reader lands on a cell, it can then say "Price, Pro plan: $12" instead of just "$12".

Cells can span: `colspan="2"` stretches a cell across two columns and `rowspan="3"` down three rows. Complex spanning makes tables hard to read and navigate; often two simple tables are clearer.

Even if you leave out `<tbody>`, the parser adds one, which matters when you write CSS like `table > tr` (it won't match). Wide tables don't fit on small screens: wrap the table in a `<div>` styled with `overflow-x: auto` so it scrolls sideways instead of breaking the layout.
concepts.code:
Plans and prices (per month)
Plan Price Projects
Free$03
Pro$12Unlimited
Prices exclude VAT.
takeaways: Tables are for tabular data only, never layout
Use caption, thead/tbody and th with scope
colspan/rowspan join cells; keep spanning simple
pitfalls: Styling `table > tr` and wondering why nothing matches: the parser added a tbody.

quiz.q: What does scope="row" on a th do?
options: Marks the cell as the header for the data cells in its row
Makes the cell span the entire row
quiz.explain: scope tells assistive technology which cells a header labels.

concepts.name: Input types and built-in validation
concepts.summary: Pick the right input type, and use required, pattern, min, max and length limits so the browser checks answers without JavaScript.
concepts.why: The right input type gives mobile users the right keyboard and gets you free validation and pickers.
concepts.body:
`<input>` has over twenty `type` values, and choosing well improves forms immediately.

- `email`, `url`, `tel`: on phones these bring up keyboards with `@`, `/` or digits. email and url are also validated.
- `number` (with `min`, `max`, `step`), `range` for a slider, `date`, `time`, `datetime-local`, `month`: native pickers.
- `checkbox`, `radio`, `color`, `file` (with `accept="image/*"` and `multiple`), `search`, `password`, `hidden`.

Checking that answers follow the rules is called **validation**, and attributes that set a rule are called **constraints**: `required`, `minlength`/`maxlength`, `min`/`max`, `step`, and `pattern`. A **pattern** is a **regular expression** — a mini-language for describing text, where `[0-9]{5}` means "five digits" — that must match the whole value. When the user submits, the cursor jumps to the first field with a problem and the browser shows its own message.

In CSS, the selectors `:invalid` and `:user-invalid` let you style fields with problems. `:user-invalid` only applies once the user has touched the field, so empty required fields aren't red when the page opens.

`autocomplete` values such as `email`, `name`, `street-address`, `new-password`, `current-password` and `one-time-code` let browsers and password managers fill fields correctly. `inputmode="numeric"` asks phones for a digit keyboard while keeping the value plain text, which is better than `type="number"` for things like card numbers and postcodes, where arrows and scroll-wheel changes make no sense.

Checks in the browser are a convenience for users, not security. Anyone can get around them, so the server must check everything again.
concepts.code:
<form>
  <label>Email <input type="email" name="email" autocomplete="email" required></label>

  <label>Age <input type="number" name="age" min="13" max="120" step="1"></label>

  <label>Postcode
    <input name="zip" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]{5}" autocomplete="postal-code"
           title="Five digits">
  </label>

  <label>Start date <input type="date" name="start" min="2026-01-01"></label>

  <label>Avatar <input type="file" name="avatar" accept="image/*"></label>

  <label>New password
    <input type="password" name="pw" minlength="12" autocomplete="new-password" required>
  </label>
  <button>Save</button>
</form>
takeaways: Specific input types give the right mobile keyboard and native pickers
required, pattern, min/max and minlength validate before submit
autocomplete values help browsers fill in forms
Always validate again on the server
pitfalls: Using type="number" for card numbers or postcodes; use inputmode="numeric" with pattern.

quiz.q: An input has pattern="[0-9]{3}". Which value passes validation?
quiz.explain: pattern must match the whole value, so exactly three digits.

concepts.name: Head metadata and SEO
concepts.summary: Fill the head with the viewport setting, a description, icons, the preferred address and link-preview tags that browsers and search engines rely on.
concepts.why: Missing head tags are why sites look tiny on phones, show ugly link previews or rank poorly.
concepts.body:
Beyond `charset` and `title`, a few more tags in the head belong on every page. Most are **meta tags**: `<meta>` elements that describe the page.

- `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` tells phones to lay the page out at the screen's real width. Without it, phones draw the page as if it were about 980 pixels wide and shrink it down, so text is tiny and CSS rules written for small screens don't apply as expected.
- `<meta name="description" content="...">` is the snippet search engines often show under your title. Write one sentence per page.
- `<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">` sets the **favicon**, the icon on the browser tab; add `<link rel="apple-touch-icon">` for home screens.
- `<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/page">` names the preferred URL when the same content can be reached at several URLs.
- `<link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles.css">` loads a CSS file, called a **stylesheet**. The browser waits for stylesheets in the head before drawing the page, which is what you want for your main CSS.

**Open Graph** tags (`og:title`, `og:description`, `og:image`, `og:url`) control the preview card when someone shares the link in chat apps and social networks; `twitter:card` refines it on X.

`<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` keeps a page out of search results. `<meta name="theme-color">` tints the browser's toolbar on phones. Note that `<meta name="keywords">` has been ignored by major search engines for years, so don't bother.
concepts.code:
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Pricing · Acme</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Simple pricing for teams of any size. Start free.">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://acme.example/pricing">
  <link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/site.css">

  <!-- link previews in chat apps and social networks -->
  <meta property="og:title" content="Acme pricing">
  <meta property="og:description" content="Start free, upgrade when you grow.">
  <meta property="og:image" content="https://acme.example/og/pricing.png">
  <meta property="og:url" content="https://acme.example/pricing">
  <meta name="theme-color" content="#0f172a">
</head>
takeaways: The viewport meta is mandatory for mobile-friendly pages
Write a unique title and description per page
canonical picks one URL for duplicate content
Open Graph tags control link previews
pitfalls: Forgetting the viewport meta tag and then fighting small-screen CSS rules that never seem to apply on phones.

quiz.q: A page looks zoomed-out and tiny on phones although its CSS has rules for small screens. What's the most likely cause?
options: The CSS file is too large
The viewport meta tag is missing
quiz.explain: Without the viewport meta, mobile browsers lay out at a desktop width and scale down.

concepts.name: Accessibility fundamentals
concepts.summary: Make pages usable for everyone: native elements, keyboard access, visible focus, text alternatives and correct names for controls.
concepts.why: Accessible HTML is a legal requirement in many places and makes sites better for all users.
concepts.body:
**Accessibility** (a11y) means people using screen readers, only a keyboard, voice control or zoom can use your page. Most of it comes free when you use the right element.

**Use native elements.** A `<button>` is focusable, activates with Enter and Space, and is announced as a button. A `<div onclick>` does none of that. The same goes for links, inputs, checkboxes and selects.

**Everything works by keyboard.** The Tab key goes through links, buttons and form fields in the order they appear in the HTML (the **tab order**). The browser outlines the element the keyboard is on: the **focus outline**. Never remove it without a visible replacement (style `:focus-visible` instead), and keep the HTML in a sensible order rather than rearranging things on screen with CSS.

**Every button, link and field has an accessible name**, the name a screen reader announces: from its text content, its `<label>`, or `alt` for images. An icon-only button needs a name, for example visually hidden text or `aria-label="Close"`.

**Structure is navigation**: a sensible heading hierarchy, landmarks (`main`, `nav`), and lists for lists. Screen-reader users jump by these.

Other essentials:

- Set `lang` on `<html>`.
- Don't convey meaning by colour alone; add text or icons.
- Keep the contrast between text and background at least 4.5:1, the level that **WCAG**, the web's accessibility guidelines, asks for.
- Add captions to video.
- Add a **skip link** ("Skip to content") as the first thing the Tab key reaches.

Test by unplugging the mouse and tabbing through the page, and by running a checker such as **Lighthouse**, built into Chrome's developer tools. Automated tools catch roughly a third of issues; keyboard and screen-reader testing finds the rest.

Skip to content
...

Inbox

Archive

Error: the email is required.
takeaways: Native elements bring keyboard support and roles for free
Everything must be reachable and visible by keyboard
Every interactive element needs an accessible name
Never rely on colour alone
pitfalls: Setting outline: none on focus without a visible replacement.

quiz.q:
Why is
Save
an accessibility problem?
options: It isn't focusable or keyboard-operable and isn't announced as a button
quiz.explain: A div has no button role, no tab stop and no Enter/Space activation; a <button> has all three.

concepts.name: Responsive images
concepts.summary: Serve the right image file for each screen with srcset and sizes, and switch formats or crops with picture.
concepts.why: Sending a 3000-pixel image to a phone wastes data and slows the page more than almost anything else.
concepts.body: One image file can't suit both a phone and a 4K monitor. HTML lets you offer several and let the browser choose. **Resolution switching** with **srcset** and `sizes`: list the files with their real widths in pixels (`photo-480.jpg 480w, photo-1200.jpg 1200w`), and use `sizes` to tell the browser how wide the image will appear, such as `(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw`: "on screens up to 600 pixels wide, the full screen width (`100vw`); otherwise half of it". The browser multiplies that width by the screen's pixel density (many phones pack 2 or 3 real pixels into each CSS pixel) and downloads the smallest file that is sharp enough. It needs `sizes` because it picks the image before CSS layout is known. Without `sizes` it assumes `100vw`. For fixed-size images, such as an 80-pixel profile picture, list one file per pixel density instead: `srcset="a.jpg 1x, a@2x.jpg 2x"`. **The picture element** handles two other cases: - **Format switching**: `` and `` before the fallback ``; the browser takes the first type it supports. - **Art direction** (a different crop for different screens): `` serves a different crop on narrow screens. The `` inside `` is required: it's what actually appears, and it carries `alt`, `width`, `height` and `loading`. The `` elements only supply alternative URLs.
takeaways: srcset with w descriptors + sizes = browser picks the right resolution
Use 1x/2x descriptors for fixed-size images
picture + source switches formats or crops; the inner img still renders
pitfalls: Leaving out sizes with w descriptors, so the browser assumes 100vw and downloads files that are too big.

quiz.q: Why does the browser need the sizes attribute with srcset width descriptors?
options: It sets the CSS width of the image
It's required for alt text to work
It chooses an image before layout, so it needs to know the display width in advance
It tells the server how to resize the image
quiz.explain: Image selection happens early, before CSS layout is known, so sizes supplies the expected display width.

concepts.name: Video, audio and embeds
concepts.summary: Play video and audio with built-in elements, add captions with track, and show other pages safely inside yours with iframe.
concepts.why: Built-in media elements work everywhere without add-ons, but captions and iframe safety settings are easy to forget.
concepts.body:
`<video>` and `<audio>` play media without any add-ons.

- `controls` shows the browser's play/pause bar. Without it, the user can't play or pause unless you build your own buttons.
- Offer the video in several file formats with `<source src type>` children; the browser plays the first it can. MP4 (H.264) plays everywhere; WebM or AV1 files are smaller.
- `poster` sets a preview picture; `preload="none"` or `"metadata"` saves data by not downloading the video up front.
- Browsers stop media from starting on its own with sound. **Autoplay** only works reliably together with `muted`, and `playsinline` keeps iPhones from going full-screen.

**Captions** come from a `<track kind="captions" src="en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">` pointing at a **WebVTT** file, a simple text format for timed captions. They're essential for deaf users and for anyone watching without sound.

An `<iframe>` shows another web page inside a rectangle on yours, like a map, a video player or a payment form. That page runs as a complete separate page inside yours, so treat it with care:

- Give it a `title` describing its content, for screen readers.
- `loading="lazy"` waits to load frames that are off screen, which are often heavy.
- `sandbox` takes away the framed page's powers (running scripts, opening pop-ups and more); add back only what it needs, e.g. `sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin"`.
- `allow` grants features such as `fullscreen` or `autoplay`.

Sites can refuse to appear inside other pages by sending special instructions with their pages (the `X-Frame-Options` or `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors` HTTP headers), which is why some URLs show an error inside an iframe.
takeaways: Add controls, multiple sources and a poster to video
Autoplay only works muted
Captions via track and WebVTT
Give iframes a title, lazy-load them, and sandbox untrusted ones
pitfalls: Expecting autoplay with sound to work; browsers block it until the user interacts.

quiz.q: A hero video with autoplay doesn't start in Chrome. What's the likely fix?
quiz.explain: Browsers allow autoplay only for muted media (or after user interaction).

concepts.name: Loading scripts: defer, async, module
concepts.summary: Control when JavaScript downloads and runs with defer, async and type=module, and hint important resources with preload.
concepts.why: A single misplaced script tag can hold up the page for seconds; the right attribute fixes it for free.
concepts.body:
A **script** is a JavaScript program that runs in the page. A plain `<script src="app.js">` in the head is **parser-blocking**: the browser stops building the page, downloads the script, runs it, then carries on. Users stare at a blank screen meanwhile. Two attributes fix this for scripts in their own files.

- `defer`: download while the browser keeps reading the page, then run once the whole page has been read, in the order the scripts appear, just before `DOMContentLoaded` (the browser's signal that the page is fully built). Right for almost all app code, because every element exists when it runs.
- `async`: download while the page is read and run as soon as it arrives, in any order, possibly before the page is fully read. Right for independent scripts like visitor statistics.

`<script type="module">` loads a JavaScript **module**: a script file that can bring in code from other files with `import`. Modules are **deferred automatically** and run only once, even if included twice. Add `async` to a module to run it as soon as it and the files it imports are ready. `<script nomodule>` is a fallback for browsers without module support, which today is effectively none.

Scripts written directly between `<script>` tags, with no `src`, ignore `defer` and run immediately (unless they're modules).

**Resource hints** in the head start downloads early. A **resource** here is any file the page loads: CSS, scripts, images, fonts.

- `<link rel="preload" href="font.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>`: download a file needed soon that the browser would only find late, such as a font named inside a CSS file.
- `<link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/chart.js">`: download a module ahead of time and prepare it.
- `<link rel="preconnect" href="https://cdn.example">`: connect to another website early, before the first file is requested from it.

Overusing preload backfires: everything preloaded competes for the connection with what's actually urgent.
concepts.code:
<head>
  <!-- Blocks parsing until downloaded and run: avoid -->
  <!-- <script src="/js/app.js"></script> -->

  <!-- Runs after parsing, in order: good default for app code -->
  <script src="/js/vendor.js" defer></script>
  <script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>

  <!-- Runs whenever it arrives: independent third-party code -->
  <script src="https://analytics.example/a.js" async></script>

  <!-- ES module: deferred automatically -->
  <script type="module" src="/js/main.js"></script>

  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
  <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
</head>
takeaways: Plain scripts in the head stop the page from being built until they've run
defer = after parsing, in order; async = whenever ready, any order
Module scripts are deferred by default
Preload only the few files that are urgent and found late
pitfalls: Using async for scripts that depend on each other; their order isn't guaranteed.

quiz.q: app.js needs lib.js to have run first. Which loading keeps the order and doesn't block parsing?
options: Both as plain scripts at the top of head
quiz.explain: Deferred scripts run in document order after parsing; async scripts run in arrival order.

concepts.name: ARIA roles, states and live regions
concepts.summary: Use ARIA attributes to describe custom widgets and dynamic changes that native HTML can't express, and know when not to.
concepts.why: Custom components like tabs, menus and toasts are only accessible if their roles and states are exposed.
concepts.body:
**ARIA** (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) adds attributes that change what assistive technology is told about an element. It changes only what an element is announced as (its meaning), never how it behaves: `role="button"` doesn't let the keyboard reach a div or press it.

That's why the **first rule of ARIA** is: don't use it if a native element does the job. A `<button>` beats `<div role="button" tabindex="0">` plus key handlers every time.

When you do build custom widgets, ARIA comes in three kinds:

- **Roles**: what something is, e.g. `role="tablist"`, `role="tab"`, `role="tabpanel"`, `role="alert"`.
- **Properties**: relationships and names: `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-controls`.
- **States**: current status, which your JavaScript must keep updating: `aria-expanded`, `aria-selected`, `aria-checked`, `aria-current="page"`, `aria-invalid`.

**Live regions** announce changes on the page without moving the keyboard focus (the spot where key presses go). Put text into an element with `aria-live="polite"` (announced when the user is idle) or `role="alert"` (assertive, immediate) and screen readers read it. The region must already be on the page *before* you change its text.

`aria-hidden="true"` hides decorative content from assistive technology, but never put it on something focusable. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide documents the expected roles and keyboard behaviour for tabs, menus, comboboxes and more; follow it rather than inventing your own.

takeaways: No ARIA is better than bad ARIA: prefer native elements
ARIA changes what is announced, not how things behave
Update states like aria-expanded from JavaScript whenever they change
Live regions must exist before their content changes
pitfalls: Adding role="button" to a div and forgetting tabindex and Enter/Space handling.

quiz.q: What does adding role="button" to a <div> give you?
options: Focus, keyboard activation and the button role
Only the button role announced to assistive technology
quiz.explain: ARIA changes semantics only; focus and keyboard behaviour must be added by you.

concepts.name: Dialog, details and popover
concepts.summary: Build pop-up windows, open/close sections and menus with dialog, details/summary and the popover attribute instead of your own JavaScript.
concepts.why: Native interactive elements handle focus, Escape and stacking for you, which custom modals routinely get wrong.
concepts.body:
HTML now covers interactions that used to need lots of JavaScript.

**details and summary** make a **disclosure widget**, a section that opens and closes when clicked: `<summary>` is the always-visible toggle, the rest shows when `open`. No script required, keyboard accessible, searchable with find-in-page. Several `<details>` with the same `name` attribute form an exclusive accordion: opening one closes the others.

**dialog** is a native modal or non-modal box.

- The JavaScript command `dialog.showModal()` opens it as a **modal**: it's placed in the **top layer**, above everything else; the rest of the page can't be clicked; the keyboard focus moves inside; and Escape closes it. Style the dimmed background with `::backdrop`.
- `dialog.show()` opens it non-modally; `dialog.close(value)` closes it.
- A `<form method="dialog">` inside closes the dialog on submit and sets `dialog.returnValue` to the submitting button's value.

**popover** is an attribute that turns any element into a popup in the top layer: `<div popover id="menu">`. A button with `popovertarget="menu"` toggles it, with no JavaScript. `popover` (auto) popovers use **light dismiss**: clicking outside or pressing Escape closes them, and opening one closes other auto popovers. `popover="manual"` stays open until closed explicitly, for toasts.

Prefer dialog for anything the user must answer, and popover for menus, tooltips and pickers. Neither can end up hidden behind other content, because the top layer always wins.

takeaways: details/summary = disclosure with no JS; shared name = accordion
showModal() gives top layer, inert background, Escape to close
`<form method="dialog">` closes the dialog and sets returnValue
popover + popovertarget = light-dismiss popups with no JS
pitfalls: Opening a modal with dialog.show() and wondering why the page behind stays interactive.

quiz.q: What does a <form method="dialog"> inside a <dialog> do when submitted?
options: Closes the dialog and sets returnValue to the button's value
Sends a POST request to the current URL
quiz.explain: method=dialog closes the enclosing dialog without a network request.

concepts.name: Templates and custom elements
concepts.summary: Reuse chunks of HTML with template and slot, and create your own elements with custom elements and shadow DOM.
concepts.why: Web components work with any JavaScript framework or none, which makes them the built-in way to share page widgets.
concepts.body:
**template** holds HTML that stays switched off: the browser reads it but doesn't show it, scripts inside don't run and images don't load. JavaScript can copy its `.content` with `template.content.cloneNode(true)` to stamp out as many copies as needed, which is faster and safer than gluing HTML together as text.

**Custom elements** let you invent new tags, like `<user-card>`. In JavaScript you write a class — a blueprint describing how every such element behaves — that builds on the built-in `HTMLElement`, and register it with `customElements.define("user-card", UserCard)`. Names must contain a hyphen, so they never clash with future HTML elements. Special methods of the class run when the element is added to the page (`connectedCallback`), removed (`disconnectedCallback`), or when one of the attributes it watches, listed in `static observedAttributes`, changes (`attributeChangedCallback`).

**Shadow DOM** gives an element its own private, hidden tree of elements: `this.attachShadow({ mode: "open" })`. Styles inside don't leak out and the page's styles don't leak in (though settings children pick up from their parents, like the font, and CSS variables still pass through). A `<slot>` in the shadow tree shows the elements written between the custom element's own tags; named slots (`<slot name="title">`) take children with a matching `slot` attribute.

You can also write the shadow tree directly in HTML with `<template shadowrootmode="open">`, so components whose HTML arrives ready-made from the server appear before any JavaScript runs.

A custom element can appear in the page before its script has loaded: it shows as a plain element and is switched on (upgraded) once the definition arrives. Style that waiting state with the `:not(:defined)` selector to avoid a flash of unstyled content.
concepts.code: Ada Wrote the first program.
takeaways: template content is read but stays switched off until copied
Custom element names must contain a hyphen
Shadow DOM keeps styles inside; slots show the element's own children
A shadow tree written in HTML (shadowrootmode) appears without JavaScript
pitfalls: Expecting the page's CSS classes to style elements inside a shadow tree.

quiz.q: Why must custom element names contain a hyphen?
options: The parser uses it to detect void elements
So they can never collide with current or future standard elements
quiz.explain: Standard elements never contain hyphens, so hyphenated names are reserved for authors.

concepts.name: How browsers parse HTML
concepts.summary: Understand the HTML parser's error recovery, implied tags and tree construction, and how the tree it builds can differ from the HTML you write.
concepts.why: Knowing what the parser does explains mystery elements, broken templates and why HTML inserted from JavaScript sometimes behaves oddly.
concepts.body:
When a browser reads your HTML it builds a tree of elements in memory, the **DOM** (Document Object Model); JavaScript reads and changes the page through that tree, and the developer tools show it. HTML parsing is precisely specified, including how to handle broken markup, so every modern browser builds the same tree from the same bytes. That spec has a few behaviours every expert should know. **First reading, then building.** The file arrives as bytes, which are turned into text using the page's encoding (taken from a marker at the very start of the file, the server's `charset` setting, or a `` within the first 1024 bytes). The text is cut into tags and text, which are fed to a tree builder. The builder tracks where it is with **insertion modes** such as "in head", "in body" and "in table". **Implied tags.** The parser inserts ``, ``, `` and `` if missing, and many end tags are optional: `

`, ``, ``, `` close automatically when a sibling starts. **Error recovery.** Tags closed in the wrong order, such as ``, are repaired by a set of steps called the adoption agency algorithm. Content that can't go inside a table is **foster-parented**: it's placed before the table instead. That's why text typed between `` elements appears above the table. **Raw text elements.** Inside `` inside JavaScript written in the page ends the script early. Escape it as `<\/script>`. **Scripts pause parsing.** A plain script must run before reading continues, because it could call `document.write`, an old JavaScript command that writes extra HTML straight into the page at that point. Meanwhile the **preload scanner** reads ahead and starts downloading images and scripts anyway, which is why files written in the HTML load faster than ones added later by JavaScript. Finally, setting an element's `innerHTML` from JavaScript (a property that replaces the element's contents with HTML given as text) runs the same parser on a piece of HTML, but `

Missing html/head/body/tbody tags are inserted for you
Stray content in tables is foster-parented before the table
</script> inside an inline script ends it: escape it

quiz.q: Text placed directly between two <tr> elements ends up where in the DOM?
quiz.explain: Foster parenting moves content that isn't allowed in table context to just before the table.

concepts.name: Loading performance in markup
concepts.summary: Tune what the browser downloads first and how fast the page appears, with fetchpriority, lazy loading, decoding hints and the critical rendering path.
concepts.why: How fast the main content appears, and whether the page jumps while loading, mostly depend on how files are referenced in your HTML.
concepts.body: The browser turns HTML into pixels through the **critical rendering path**: read the HTML and build the DOM; download the CSS and build the **CSSOM**, the matching tree for styles (nothing is drawn until it's ready); run any scripts that hold up the page; then work out the layout and paint. Your HTML decides what lands on that path. **Priorities.** Browsers decide what to download first by rules of thumb: CSS and page-holding scripts high, images low until it turns out they're on screen. How soon the biggest image or text block on screen appears is called **Largest Contentful Paint** (LCP), a key speed score. `fetchpriority="high"` on the big image at the top tells the browser up front that it's the LCP element; `fetchpriority="low"` demotes, say, off-screen carousel slides. It works on ``, ``, `
takeaways: Put the LCP image in the HTML with fetchpriority="high" and never lazy
The preload scanner can only find resources in markup
Sizes on media prevent layout shift
Measure LCP and CLS before and after changes
pitfalls: Setting the big top image as a CSS background, hiding it from the preload scanner.

quiz.q: Which change most likely improves LCP when the hero is ?
options: Moving the image into a CSS background
quiz.explain: Lazy loading delays the in-viewport hero; high priority fetches it first.

concepts.name: Form submission and constraint validation API
concepts.summary: Know exactly how forms package and send data, and control validation from JavaScript with the constraint validation API and FormData.
concepts.why: File uploads, custom error messages and progressive enhancement all depend on these details.
concepts.body:
When a form is sent, the browser collects the fields that count (named, not disabled, and ticked if a checkbox or radio button) and packs them according to the form's **enctype** attribute:

- `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` (the default): `name=Ada+L&tags=a&tags=b` — spaces become `+` and other special characters become `%` codes. With `method="get"` this becomes the query string.
- `multipart/form-data`: each field travels as its own separate part, labelled with its type. Required for `<input type="file">`; with the default, only the file name is sent.
- `text/plain`: for testing only; the receiving side can't reliably read it back.

A submit button's `name=value` is included only for the button that was clicked, and a button can change where and how the form is sent with `formaction`, `formmethod` and `formnovalidate`. Disabled controls are never sent; use `readonly` if the value must be submitted.

**The constraint validation API** lets JavaScript use the browser's built-in checks. Each control has `validity` (flags such as `valueMissing`, `patternMismatch`, `tooShort`, `customError`), `validationMessage`, `checkValidity()` and `reportValidity()`. `setCustomValidity("message")` marks a control invalid with your text; set it back to `""` or the field stays invalid forever. The `novalidate` attribute on the form turns off the browser's own error pop-ups while keeping the checks available to JavaScript, which is how custom error messages are built.

`new FormData(form)` captures exactly what a native submit would send, and `fetch(url, { method: "POST", body: formData })` (JavaScript's way to send a request) sends it as multipart. Listening to the form's `submit` event and calling `requestSubmit()`, rather than `submit()`, keeps validation and submit handlers in play.
concepts.code:
<form id="f" action="/api/profile" method="post" enctype="multipart/form-data" novalidate>
  <input name="username" required minlength="3">
  <input name="avatar" type="file" accept="image/*">
  <input name="confirm" placeholder="type DELETE">
  <button name="intent" value="save">Save</button>
</form>
<script>
  const f = document.getElementById("f");
  f.addEventListener("submit", async (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    const c = f.elements.confirm;
    c.setCustomValidity(c.value === "DELETE" ? "" : "Type DELETE to confirm");
    if (!f.reportValidity()) return;      // shows first error, focuses it
    const data = new FormData(f, e.submitter); // includes intent=save
    const res = await fetch(f.action, { method: "POST", body: data });
    console.log(res.status);
  });
</script>
takeaways: File uploads need enctype="multipart/form-data"
Disabled controls are not submitted; readonly ones are
setCustomValidity("") clears a custom error
FormData(form, submitter) mirrors a native submit
pitfalls: Calling setCustomValidity with a message and never resetting it to an empty string.

quiz.q: A form with the default enctype has a file input. What does the server receive for it?
options: A multipart part with the file
quiz.explain: Only multipart/form-data carries file contents; urlencoded sends just the file name.
